newsitem.title: SPAIN: Colombia determined to reinstate extradition.
newsitem.headline: Colombia determined to reinstate extradition.

text.p: Colombia said on Sunday it was determined to reinstate extradition as soon as possible as a measure to fight drug-trafficking.

"This is now just a question of time. It could be this month or the next, but Colombia is disposed to re-establish extradition," Colombian Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia told Reuters in an interview during a visit to Madrid.
Colombia, under pressure from the United States, is trying to end a ban on extradition of drug lords and other criminals.
Extradition was abolished in 1991 after hundreds of people were killed in a campaign of violence that was started in the late 1980s by drug lords opposed to the measure.
The issue has been the subject of hot debate among Colombian legislators.
Last week the Senate rejected a proposal by President Ernesto Samper to reinstate extradition but the government is hopeful a draft law will be approved by Congress on Tuesday.
"Colombia's commitment in the fight against drug-traffickers is total and definitive and the last of the pieces is extradition," Mejia said.
"If it doesn't pass in this legislature, the government is ready for it to be in Congress in the next legislature."

Mejia said she hoped the delay in re-establishing extradition would not worsen already precarious relations with the United States, which has cut off aid to Colombia for a second consecutive year for failing to take adequate anti-drug measures.

"We are not on an obstacle course. But if this makes it so they decertify us once again, it would be lamentable, but Colombia has its own conviction about the need for re-establishing extradition," she said.
Mejia was travelling with Samper, who had a private meeting with Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar on Sunday.
